title: Coherence
author: Nick Hart
summary: The second post in Nick Hart's six sense making disciplines series, adapted from Richard Claydon, addresses coherence: the discipline that reduces fragmentation across time, teams and decisions. Hart argues that in schools incoherence accumulates through small disconnections such as misaligned initiatives, policies built on different assumptions, and well-meant new ideas. His move is to treat coherence as deliberate, repeated acts of interpretation that widen the frame in which leaders understand problems. He sets out four strategies: iceberg systems thinking, asking how a proposal relates to existing priorities, backtracking from actions to the beliefs that produce them, and mapping second-order consequences. He argues these strategies do integrative work, preventing the cycle of 'fixes that fail' in which yesterday's solutions become today's problems. Used well, they slow premature solution-building and allow organisational learning to compound rather than reset.
points: Hart argues that incoherence in schools builds through small disconnections, including the natural emergence of new ideas from well-meaning people, rather than through dramatic failures.
Iceberg systems thinking moves teams from incidents to patterns, structures and assumptions, because today's problems are often the result of yesterday's quick fixes.
Tracing behaviour back to the beliefs that generate it makes disagreement analytical rather than personal, in a systemic view where patterns stem from structures rather than individual intent.
Practical prompts include asking who else a decision will affect, how an idea might be misinterpreted, testing it with the person most likely to disagree, and running a pre-mortem.
quotes: If clarity reduces ambiguity about direction, coherence reduces fragmentation across time, teams and decisions. Rather than treating problems as isolated events, the coherence discipline shapes how leaders connect actions to patterns and decisions to structures. It strengthens alignment so that collective work does not drift into disconnected activity.

Coherence is produced through deliberate acts of interpretation, exercised repeatedly and made visible to others. In complex systems, leaders cannot control every variable but they can widen the frame within which problems are understood.

Often, today’s problems are the result of yesterday’s solutions. Quick fixes relieve pressure in the short term but can generate unintended consequences that reappear later in altered form. When teams remain at the level of events, they solve repeatedly without learning.

Fragmentation often begins with treating decisions as independent. Leaders practising coherence routinely ask how a new proposal, issue or idea connects to existing priorities and structures. Work that is not integrated at the point of decision must be reconciled later, often at greater cost.

Surfacing that logic makes disagreement analytical rather than personal. In systemic terms, there is no blame; patterns of behaviour are often produced by structures and assumptions rather than individual intent.

In complex systems, cause and effect are not closely related in time and space. Leaders practising coherence consider how decisions will interact with other parts of the system and how effects might emerge later and elsewhere.
When coherence is weak, leaders experience repeated rework. The same categories of problem recur. Standards drift.
